title: Infrastructure Engineering: GPU Fleet, Capacity & CI/CD Ops Guide
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This document is the canonical operations guide for Redwood Inference infrastructure teams responsible for the GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines and on-call runbooks. It consolidates standards, ownership, concrete thresholds, and step-by-step procedures for common day-2 and incident scenarios.

Scope

- GPU fleet lifecycle (provisioning, decommissioning, upgrades)
- Capacity planning and autoscaling policies
- Cloud account layout, VPC and cross-account networking patterns
- Terraform/IaC module conventions and registry usage
- CI/CD build and deployment pipelines for infra changes and runtime images
- Runbooks for the most common GPU/infra incidents

Owner & Contact

- Service owner: Infra - GPU & Capacity (infra-gpu@redwood.internal)
- Primary on-call: infra-sre rotation (pager duty)
- Document author: Aisha Patel
- Reviewers: Ravi Kapoor, Elena García, Marco Chen

High-level Goals & SLOs

- Node availability SLO: 99.9% per region for GPU pool control plane and provisioning APIs.
- GPU pod scheduling success: >= 99.5% within 30s under normal load.
- Capacity headroom: maintain >= 15% spare capacity relative to predicted 7-day peak.
- Time-to-scale (horizontal): average < 120s for autoscaler-triggered provisioning (cold start to ready).

Ownership & Component Map

- infra-gpu-team: GPU host pool, node images, node lifecycle automation, capacity planning.
- infra-networking: VPC design, cross-account peering, Cloud NAT, shared services VPC.
- infra-iac: terraform modules, module registry, CI pipelines for state changes.
- infra-ci: pipeline templates, build images, gating and policy checks.

GPU Fleet & Capacity

Overview

GPU fleet consists of regionally scoped node pools (prod-us, prod-eu, dedicated-us, staging) managed by Kubernetes clusters with GPU node groups. Nodes run a minimal host image with: NVIDIA drivers, containerd, kubelet config tuned for low-latency inference, and the Redwood inference host agent.

Pool naming convention (examples):
- prod-us-gpu-a100-v2
- prod-eu-gpu-h100-v1
- dedicated-<customer>-us-gpu-a100

Capacity planning rules

1. Baseline: set pool target capacity = 1.2 * 7-day rolling average of peak hourly usage.
2. Headroom: maintain at least 15% headroom; if forecasted headroom < 10% for next 72h, open capacity incident and schedule procurement/scale.
3. Buffer for scheduled maintenance: reserve 5% extra capacity when performing rolling kernel/drivers upgrades.
4. Prewarm for quarterly marketing events or known traffic spikes using manual scale policy 24-72 hours in advance.

Autoscaling policy (recommended template)

- Scale up trigger: pending pods for 3 consecutive 30s checks AND node CPU >= 80% or GPU util >= 70% for 2 minutes.
- Scale down trigger: node idle for 15 minutes and cluster utilization < 40% for 30 minutes.
- Max scale step: 25% of pool size or 10 nodes (whichever smaller) to avoid noisy neighbor spikes.

Key Metrics & Alerts

- gpu_pool_utilization (%) \u2014 warn at 75%, sev at 90%
- pending_gpu_pods \u2014 warn at > 5 sustained for 5 minutes, sev at > 20
- node_provision_time (s) \u2014 warn if median > 180s, sev if median > 300s
- GPU_driver_mismatch \u2014 sev immediate (driver mismatch prevents pod scheduling)
- disk_pressure_node_count \u2014 warn at > 2 nodes, sev at > 5

Cloud Accounts & Networking

Account structure

- org-root: billing and security audit accounts.
- shared-services (centralized logging, monitoring, CI runners).
- dev, staging, prod per region (prod-us, prod-eu, prod-apac).
- dedicated customer accounts (for Redwood Private / Dedicated deployments) linked via cross-account roles.

VPC design (standard pattern)

- Shared-services VPC (centralized NAT, bastion jump hosts, monitoring endpoints).
- Regional inference VPCs: split subnets by purpose (control-plane, workload-private, egress).
- Use private subnets for GPU nodes; public subnets only for bastions and load balancers.

Networking best practices

- Use VPC peering or Transit Gateway for cross-account connectivity depending on scale.
- Enforce egress via Cloud NAT for controlled outbound IPs; tag nat-gateway resources for cost attribution.
- IP addressing: standard /16 per region, /24 per AZ workload subnet.
- Security groups: least privilege for agent-to-control-plane and metric-export ports (e.g., 9090, 8125).

Terraform & IaC Modules

Module registry & conventions

- Modules live in git under infra-iac/modules (aws-vpc, k8s-node-group-gpu, iam-roles, cloudwatch-agent).
- Module versioning: semantic version tags (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH); releases via CI tagging pipeline.
- Naming: resources should use the pattern: r-{env}-{service}-{region}-{short}.

Required module characteristics

- Inputs and outputs documented in module README.md (examples included).
- Minimal side effects: avoid creating implicit IAM policies or service-linked roles unless explicit.
- State handling: remote state in centralized backend per-account and per-environment.

Example usage (terraform snippet)

```hcl
module \"gpu_node_group\" {
  source = \"git::ssh://git@repo/infra-iac/modules.git//k8s-node-group-gpu?ref=v1.4.0\"
  name   = \"prod-us-gpu-a100-v2\"
  region = \"us-west-2\"
  instance_type = \"p4d.24xlarge\"
  desired_capacity = 40
}
```

IaC PR requirements (CI gating)

1. All changes must run `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate`.
2. Plan must be produced with `-out` and attached to the PR as an artifact.
3. Approval from infra-iac reviewers for any resource changes that cost > $100/month or change networking/IAM.
4. State migration plans for breaking changes must include a rollback plan in PR description.

CI/CD & Build

Pipeline overview

- infra-ci pipelines are defined in gitlab/github actions under infra/ci.
- Two main pipelines: `infra-plan-apply` (for IaC) and `node-image-builder` (for host images).
- All pipelines run in shared-services account runners with ephemeral credentials via OIDC.

Pipeline stages (IaC)

1. Lint & test: `tflint`, `checkov`, policy-as-code (conftest)
2. Plan: produce `terraform plan` artifact for reviewers
3. Gate: auto-approve non-prod changes with low-risk labels, require human approval for prod
4. Apply: executed by infra-ops bot or on-call with MFA for production accounts

Host image build (node image)

- Base: minimal OS (Bottlerocket or Ubuntu LTS), NVIDIA driver bundle, container runtime config.
- Image pipeline produces signed AMIs and a signed manifest stored in s3://infra-artifacts/images/
- Rolling deploy: use nodegroup blue/green or cordon/evict pattern with 1AZ at a time.

Build image hardening checklist

- Non-root default for agent processes where possible
- Signed artifacts and immutable AMI tags (no latest in prod)
- Up-to-date security packages and CVE scan report attached to image artifact

Runbooks (operational procedures)

1) High GPU Utilization / Capacity Exhaustion

- Symptoms: gpu_pool_utilization >= 90% AND pending_gpu_pods > 10
- Immediate actions:
  1. Pager alerts on-call.
  2. Check forecast dashboard and recent autoscaler events (`kubectl get hpa`, autoscaler logs).
  3. If autoscaler failed: inspect infra-ci plan and node provisioning logs, restart cloud autoscaler controller pod.
  4. If demand spike: trigger manual scale (increase desired_capacity by 15-25%) and create capacity incident ticket.
  5. Communicate to product teams via #prod-gpu-alerts with ETA.

2) Node Provisioning Failure (slow cold starts)

- Symptoms: node_provision_time median > 300s or nodes in NotReady
- Steps:
  1. Check cloud provider provisioning status and quota.
  2. Validate AMI/host image health (canary AMI test results in s3 manifest).
  3. Restart kubelet or container runtime on affected host via SSM.
  4. If root cause is driver mismatch, rollback to last-known-good AMI and start a controlled reimage.

3) GPU Driver Mismatch / Incompatible Kernel

- Immediate severity. Pods will fail scheduling or crash.
- Steps:
  1. Mark pool as degraded in capacity dashboard.
  2. Roll back to a previous AMI (documented in image manifest).
  3. Patch the driver build pipeline and publish new signed AMI once validated.

4) Networking / Cross-account Connectivity Degraded

- Symptoms: control-plane cannot reach node agents, metrics missing for a region.
- Steps:
  1. Validate Transit Gateway peering and route tables.
  2. Check NAT gateway quotas and interface statuses.
  3. Use VPC flow logs to identify blocked CIDR ranges.
  4. If routes were changed by a recent PR, rollback Terraform change immediately.

Incident Postmortem Template

- Summary (1\u20132 lines)
- Impact (customers, services, duration)
- Timeline of events (timestamped)
- Root cause analysis
- Remediation and follow-ups (owners and due dates)
- Lessons learned and SLO changes required

Runbook maintenance

- Runbooks are reviewed after every Sev2+ incident and at least quarterly by owners.
- Ownership: each runbook has an owner field at the top; infra-gpu owner must update contact list.

Operational Playbook: Routine Tasks

- Weekly: capacity forecast refresh, autoscaler health check, spot instance reclaim metrics review.
- Monthly: node-image CVE scan and patch cycle, kernel/drivers staging run, and capacity dry-run.
- Quarterly: full disaster recovery test for multi-AZ failover and cross-region scaling.

Common Troubleshooting Commands (examples)

- kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=autoscaler -o wide
- kubectl describe node <node-name> | egrep -i "conditions|gpu"
- aws ec2 describe-instance-status --instance-ids <id> --region <region>
- terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out=plan.out

Documentation & Team Wiki Links

- GPU onboarding checklist: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-onboarding-checklist
- IaC module registry: git@repo/infra-iac/modules
- Image manifest S3: s3://infra-artifacts/images/manifest.json (read-only for most users)
- Oncall rota and runbook index: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks

FAQ & Known Tradeoffs

- Q: Why maintain 15% headroom?
  A: Balances cost vs. risk \u2014 15% covers most sudden spikes and allows time for autoscaler to provision without user-facing errors.

- Q: When should we prefer dedicated customer accounts?
  A: For compliance or data residency requirements or when customers request physical isolation; otherwise use tenancy features and IAM boundaries in shared accounts.
